title: Fine-Tuning vs RAG vs Prompting: Choosing the Right Intervention
excerpt: Choose prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning by diagnosing evidence and behavior failures, then compare interventions with representative data and clear evaluations.
content:
Choosing between prompting, retrieval-augmented generation, and fine-tuning starts with diagnosing the failure. A model that lacks a current product document has a different problem from a model that receives the right document but repeatedly formats the answer incorrectly. Applying the same intervention to both can make a system more complicated without making its decisions more dependable.

The practical distinction is where you want to change the system: the instructions and examples supplied for this request, the evidence made available at inference time, or the model parameters learned from training examples. These mechanisms can be combined. The architecture should follow measured failure categories rather than a presumed progression from prompting to something more sophisticated.

## Separate missing evidence from incorrect behavior

For an illustrative diagnostic, review failed tasks with their complete inputs, retrieved passages, generated outputs, and acceptance checks. Assign a provisional cause before changing the model:

| Observed failure | First experiment to try | What the experiment tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Necessary information was absent | Supply verified evidence directly | Whether missing context explains the failure |
| Relevant evidence exists but was not retrieved | Improve ingestion or retrieval | Whether the search stage loses the answer |
| Evidence is present but instructions are ambiguous | Clarify the task and add examples | Whether the desired behavior is sufficiently specified |
| A stable response pattern remains inconsistent | Evaluate supervised fine-tuning | Whether learned adaptation improves that behavior |
| Required arithmetic or authorization is wrong | Enforce it in application code | Whether a deterministic control should own the decision |

This table is a proposed investigation procedure, not a universal classification of model errors. A single task can have several causes. For instance, retrieving an outdated API guide and failing to mention its version creates both an evidence problem and a reporting problem.

Avoid diagnosing from the final answer alone. A fluent incorrect answer does not reveal whether the model lacked evidence, ignored evidence, or followed a misleading instruction. Preserve the intermediate artifacts needed to distinguish those possibilities.

## Prompting changes the request rather than the weights

A prompt can specify the objective, constraints, response structure, examples, and information to use. Anthropic's prompting guidance emphasizes clarity, explicit instructions, and relevant examples. Those recommendations provide a sensible baseline; they do not establish that one prompt pattern performs best across all models. [Anthropic prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices).

For the diagnostic procedure here, create the smallest prompt that makes the task contract inspectable. Specify what evidence is required, how to express uncertainty, and which output fields are mandatory. Add examples that demonstrate difficult boundaries rather than ten nearly identical easy cases.

Treat the prompt as a versioned application input. When it changes, compare the new version against the same held-out tasks. Otherwise an apparent improvement may come from changing the evaluation examples at the same time.

Prompting is particularly attractive while requirements are changing because edits are easy to inspect and reverse. Its limits are also operational: instructions and examples consume context, and a longer prompt does not automatically resolve contradictions. If the specification itself is inconsistent, training on it can preserve that inconsistency instead of fixing it.

## RAG changes the evidence available for this answer

The original RAG paper combines a pretrained generator with an external retrieval index and trains retrieval-augmented models. This is an important historical detail: retrieval and fine-tuning are not intrinsically competing categories. A system can use both. The paper's benchmark findings describe its research setup, not the expected improvement of an arbitrary production knowledge base. [Lewis and colleagues: Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401).

For a proposed production design, retrieval is useful when answers need identifiable source documents, tenant-specific knowledge, or information that changes independently of the model deployment. The application can select a current document version, retain its identifier, and expose the supporting passage alongside the answer.

Retrieval does not guarantee that the correct evidence reaches the generator. Parsing, chunking, indexing, permissions, candidate selection, and context packing can each remove essential information. Anthropic's contextual-retrieval account illustrates one such failure: a chunk can lose the surrounding information needed to interpret it. Its proposed contextualization method addresses retrieval representation; its reported results should be understood as provider experiments. [Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://www.anthropic.com/research/contextual-retrieval).

Before blaming the generator, compare its answer with the actual evidence packet. If the missing exception never entered that packet, fine-tuning the answer style is unlikely to repair the retrieval boundary. Review [RAG chunking and document ingestion](/blog/rag-chunking-document-ingestion) before adding more model adaptation.

## Fine-tuning changes a learned response distribution

Supervised fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model using examples of inputs and desired outputs. Parameter-efficient methods change how adaptation is represented: LoRA freezes the original weights and trains low-rank update matrices. Its paper demonstrates an adaptation technique, not a guarantee that any small dataset will produce a useful specialist. [Hu and colleagues: LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685).

Fine-tuning can affect both behavior and factual responses, so “fine-tuning is only for style” is too restrictive. The engineering question is whether the knowledge or behavior should be maintained through a training lifecycle. A mutable policy that needs source attribution may be easier to operate as retrieved evidence than as information implicitly reflected in a checkpoint.

A fine-tuning experiment also needs an example contract. Google's supervised-tuning documentation stresses representative production inputs, correct target outputs, and validation data. It explicitly discusses maintaining the same input structure between training and production. [Google: preparing supervised fine-tuning data](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/tuning/supervised-tuning/prepare-data).

For the proposed evaluation here, that means a training example should include the evidence the deployed model will actually receive. If training answers rely on context omitted from the input, the dataset can reward unsupported inference. A large pile of resolved tickets is not automatically a training set: it may contain stale policies, copied mistakes, missing attachments, and inconsistent reviewer decisions.

## Work through a hypothetical migration assistant

Imagine an assistant for a fictional SDK called Orion. It must identify the API version in a code sample, retrieve the matching migration guide, and produce a review packet containing deprecated calls, suggested replacements, evidence links, and unresolved questions. All product details and counts in this scenario are illustrative.

A failure review finds three patterns. Some answers cite an older guide because the index does not distinguish versions. Other answers receive the correct guide but omit the evidence identifier. A third group proposes replacements for functions whose behavior is not covered in the supplied documentation.

Start with separate interventions. Add version-aware retrieval metadata and reject a document set that mixes incompatible releases. Clarify the output contract and provide examples of evidence-linked findings. Require an explicit unresolved finding when the supplied guide does not support a replacement. Validate the output fields in code rather than merely requesting valid structure.

Suppose the evidence-link behavior remains inconsistent after these changes. That is a candidate for a supervised adaptation experiment: prepare examples that demonstrate extracting migration findings from supplied evidence, preserving uncertainty, and producing the required packet. Keep the current migration documents outside the training target as a separate evidence source.

Do not train the assistant to repeat a particular replacement whenever it sees a function name. That shortcut might score well on repeated examples while failing when the SDK changes or a different tenant supplies a forked implementation. Include counterexamples where a familiar name appears in an incompatible version or lacks supporting documentation.

The proposed final system could therefore use fine-tuning for a recurring reporting task, retrieval for current version-specific facts, and deterministic validation for packet completeness. This is a design hypothesis to test, not a claim that all three components are necessary.

## Compare interventions without changing the question

Use an evaluation matrix that separates mechanisms:

- Baseline model with a clarified prompt.
- The same baseline with retrieved evidence.
- A fine-tuned model with the same clarified prompt.
- The fine-tuned model with the same retrieval pipeline.

Keep task acceptance criteria fixed. Record unsupported claims, version mismatches, missing evidence, abstentions, accepted outcomes, cost per accepted outcome, and latency. Compare results by failure category; an average can hide improved formatting alongside worse factual grounding.

Reserve tasks that differ from training examples by document version, code family, and customer context. Also hold out changes introduced after the training snapshot. Exact prompt deduplication alone cannot prevent leakage when nearly identical migration examples appear in both sets. See [building agent evaluation datasets](/blog/ai-agent-evaluation-datasets) for the broader dataset design.

Include operational costs in the decision. Retrieval requires ingestion and freshness monitoring. Fine-tuning requires dataset maintenance, training evaluation, deployment compatibility, and rollback. Prompting requires version control and regression checks. Prefer the intervention that fixes the identified failure with a maintenance burden the team can actually own.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can fine-tuning replace a knowledge base?

It can change what a model tends to answer, including factual content. That does not provide the same document-level update, access-control, or provenance interface as an external knowledge source. Decide which maintenance and evidence requirements your application needs.

### Should I fine-tune before fixing retrieval?

Only if the experiment addresses a distinct, measured problem. If required evidence is absent from the generator's input, first test what happens when the correct evidence is supplied. Otherwise you may train around a pipeline defect without resolving it.

### Is a hybrid system always best?

No. Each component adds failure modes and operational work. A clear prompt may already meet the acceptance criteria. Retain retrieval or fine-tuning only when controlled evaluation demonstrates a useful improvement or a necessary capability.
